stories.headline: Australia Opens Royal Commission Hearings on Antisemitism After Bondi Hanukkah Attack
stories.summary:
Australia's royal commission into antisemitism opened its first public hearings Monday in Sydney, with survivors and family members of victims from the December Bondi Beach Hanukkah shooting testifying about the ongoing impact of antisemitic violence and harassment. Sheina Gutnick, whose father Reuven Morrison was killed while throwing objects at the gunmen to protect others, told the commission she had received messages since the attack saying she too should have been killed. The shooting left 15 dead; gunman Sajid Akram was killed by police at the scene, and his son Naveed Akram faces 59 charges including 15 counts of murder.

Gutnick described a marked shift in the social acceptability of antisemitism since October 2023, telling the commission: 'I felt as though antisemitism was allowed to come into the open. All of a sudden it was socially, morally acceptable for antisemitic comments to be made in public discourse.' A second witness, identified only as AAL, said he was reconsidering whether Australia remained safe for his grandchildren.

The commission has received nearly 7,500 public submissions. Former High Court judge Virginia Bell, overseeing the proceedings, published an interim report last week with 14 recommendations including gun reforms and extended police protection for Jewish community events. The first block of hearings runs through May 15, focusing on lived experience of antisemitism before the commission delivers a final report on the anniversary of the attack.

Bell acknowledged a 'sharp spike' in antisemitism mirrored across Western countries and linked to 'events in the Middle East,' underscoring the global dimension of the issue. The commission's work comes as governments in Australia, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere grapple with how to respond to rising hate crimes against Jewish communities.

stories.headline: North Korean Athletes to Cross into South Korea for First Time Since 2018
stories.summary:
North Korean women's football club Naegohyang will travel to South Korea later this month to compete in the Asian Women's Champions League semi-final against Suwon on May 20, marking the first time athletes from North Korea have crossed the border since the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. Pyongyang has submitted a list of 27 players and 12 staff for the trip, and South Korea's Unification Ministry has confirmed the visit.

The rare crossing carries significant diplomatic weight. The two Koreas are technically still at war — no peace treaty was signed when the Korean War ended in 1953 — and relations have deteriorated sharply in recent years, with North Korea labeling the South its 'most hostile state' and formally abandoning any pursuit of reunification. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has sought to ease those tensions since taking office.

Naegohyang is appearing in the Asian Women's Champions League for the first time, having defeated Ho Chi Minh City of Vietnam 3-0 in the quarter-final. The winner of the semi-final will face Melbourne City or Tokyo Verdy in the final, also to be played in Suwon on May 23.

Analysts note that even limited athletic exchanges have historically served as a diplomatic opening between the two nations. The visit is being closely watched as a potential signal of whether inter-Korean dialogue may be reviving under the current South Korean administration.

stories.headline: John Sterling, Voice of the New York Yankees for 35 Years, Dies at 87
stories.summary:
John Sterling, the radio broadcaster whose voice defined New York Yankees baseball for more than three decades, died Monday at age 87. Sterling began calling Yankees games on WABC radio in 1989 and retired in April 2024, having called 5,420 regular-season games and 211 postseason contests. He worked 5,060 consecutive games between 1989 and 2019, rarely missing a broadcast.

Sterling was known nationally for his signature home run calls — personalized, theatrical exclamations tailored to individual players — and for his catchphrase 'It is high, it is far, it is gone!' He won 12 Emmy Awards over the course of his career and was widely regarded as one of the most distinctive voices in baseball broadcasting history.

A native New Yorker, Sterling became synonymous with the Yankees through their championship dynasties of the late 1990s and their subsequent decades of contention. His tenure spanned some of the franchise's most celebrated and turbulent eras, and his retirement in 2024 was treated as the end of an institution by fans across the region.

Tributes from players, broadcasters, and fans poured in following the announcement of his death. Sterling called more games for the Yankees than any other announcer in the franchise's history.

stories.headline: Nobel Laureate Narges Mohammadi Near Death in Iranian Prison, Family Says
stories.summary:
Jailed Iranian human rights campaigner and 2023 Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi has been hospitalized after a catastrophic deterioration in her health, following what her family describes as 140 days of arbitrary detention and the persistent denial of specialized medical care. Her brother Hamidreza Mohammadi, speaking from Norway, told the BBC he fears she is dying and wakes up each day "waiting for the worst call" he could receive. She was transferred from Zanjan Prison to a local hospital after suffering a suspected heart attack, having previously been found unconscious by fellow inmates.

Mohammadi, 54, has a history of serious cardiac, lung, and blood pressure conditions, including a pulmonary embolism and prior stenting and angiography. Her family says treatment at the Zanjan hospital is effectively impossible given her complex medical history and is calling for her transfer to specialists in Tehran. The head of the Nobel Peace Prize Committee, Jorgen Watne Frydnes, told Reuters her life is at risk and echoed the family's call for adequate care.

Mohammadi has been arrested 13 times over her lifetime and has been sentenced to a cumulative 31 years in prison and 154 lashes. Iranian authorities have not publicly responded to the family's account or to international calls for her release. Her brother suggested the ongoing Iran war and international focus on the Strait of Hormuz have diverted global attention from the plight of political prisoners inside the country.

stories.headline: European Leaders Converge on Armenia for Unprecedented Summits as Russia Watches
stories.summary:
More than 30 European leaders and Canada's prime minister are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, for a European Political Community summit on Monday — an extraordinary diplomatic moment for a country long considered one of Russia's closest allies in the South Caucasus. A first-ever bilateral EU-Armenia summit follows on Tuesday, attended by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. The gatherings signal Armenia's accelerating pivot away from Moscow following Russia's failure to defend it during Azerbaijan's 2023 military operation in Nagorno-Karabakh.

Armenia remains formally embedded in Russia's economic and security orbit — it is a member of Putin's Eurasian Economic Union and hosts a Russian military base — yet its parliament passed a law in March 2025 to begin the EU accession process. Armenia's foreign relations committee chairman cited the 2023 war as a turning point, saying the country "realised that the security architecture we are in was not working." The EU had brokered a border recognition deal and deployed a civilian monitoring mission that shifted public sentiment toward Europe.

The diplomatic realignment carries regional costs. Azerbaijan's parliament voted last week to suspend ties with the European Parliament over a resolution calling for the right of return of Nagorno-Karabakh Armenians and the release of Armenian prisoners. A Trump-brokered White House agreement last August between Armenia and Azerbaijan aimed to end decades of conflict, and a connectivity corridor linking the region to European markets — dubbed the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity — runs along Armenia's border with Iran. Moscow has watched the shifting alignments with evident displeasure.

stories.headline: Spirit Airlines Shutdown to Raise Fares, Strand Passengers; Refund Path Unclear for Some
stories.summary:
Spirit Airlines' abrupt shutdown is expected to push airfares higher across the industry, with analysts warning that reduced capacity in markets the carrier once served will drive up ticket prices at an already elevated baseline. A CBS News analysis of aviation analytics firm Cirium's data found average fares on routes where Spirit previously operated jumped 23%, or roughly $60 for a round trip, when the carrier exited. Overall passenger volume on those routes fell 20% as well. The shutdown compounds pressure from higher jet fuel costs tied to the Iran war.

Spirit announced Saturday that it had begun an "orderly wind-down of operations, effective immediately," after a $500 million federal bailout effort stalled. All flights have been canceled. Customers who purchased tickets with a credit or debit card are entitled to full refunds, which Spirit says it will process automatically. However, travelers who paid in cash, with vouchers, or through Spirit's loyalty points program may receive little or nothing — their cases will be determined through the bankruptcy process.

Travel experts are advising affected passengers not to cancel their tickets proactively, as doing so could forfeit protections. Instead, they recommend filing a chargeback with the card issuer on grounds of non-delivery of service. Several other airlines have announced short-term special offers for displaced Spirit customers, though the Transportation Department noted passengers will need to provide a Spirit confirmation number and proof of payment to access those fares.

stories.headline: NTSB Launches Investigation After United Airlines Plane Strikes Pole on NJ Turnpike Approach
stories.summary:
The National Transportation Safety Board announced Sunday it has opened a formal investigation into an incident in which a United Airlines Boeing 767-400, operating as Flight 169 from Venice to Newark, struck a light pole and a truck on the New Jersey Turnpike while on approach to Newark Liberty Airport. No immediate casualty figures were reported in initial coverage, but the incident prompted NTSB involvement given the proximity of a commercial wide-body aircraft to a major highway.

The Boeing 767-400 is a large twin-aisle jet commonly used on transatlantic routes. Investigators will examine flight data, crew communications, and approach procedures to determine how a commercial aircraft came close enough to the highway infrastructure to make contact. Newark Liberty Airport's approach paths run over densely populated areas of northern New Jersey, making such incidents a matter of public safety concern.

The NTSB investigation is in its early stages and no cause has been assigned. United Airlines has not yet issued a detailed public statement beyond confirming the incident. The event adds to ongoing scrutiny of aviation safety procedures at Newark, one of the busiest airports in the northeastern United States.
